currentGrants.title: High-performance compute cluster for brain science
currentGrants.description: This instrumentation grant supports the acquisition of a state-of-the-art high-performance computing cluster dedicated to brain science research. The system enables large-scale computational neuroscience modeling, deep learning experiments, and analysis of large neuroimaging datasets, providing essential infrastructure for advancing our understanding of brain function and developing next-generation AI systems.

currentGrants.title: One vision: Computational alignment of deep neural networks with humans
currentGrants.description: This project develops methods to quantify and improve alignment between deep neural networks and human visual processing. Our work reveals that current vision models process information fundamentally differently from humans. We adopt a developmental psychology approach to identify learning principles that shape human vision and incorporate these into AI training to create models that see the world as humans do. This research is crucial for building more robust AI systems and understanding brain mechanisms underlying human vision.

currentGrants.title: Brain-inspired deep learning models of visual reasoning
currentGrants.description: This project investigates the computational principles underlying visual reasoning in biological systems to develop more capable AI. We develop cognitive benchmarks that reveal systematic failures in modern deep learning systems and use insights from these failures to guide the development of brain-inspired architectures. Our work combines computational modeling, human psychophysics, and neurophysiology to identify the neural mechanisms supporting flexible visual reasoning and implement similar strategies in artificial systems.

currentGrants.title: REPRISM: Flexible embodied problem-solving by manipulating the representational prism
currentGrants.description: This Multi-University Research Initiative (MURI) investigates how agents can flexibly solve problems by manipulating their internal representations. The project explores how different representational schemes affect an agent's ability to reason, plan, and act in complex environments. Our contribution focuses on developing vision systems that can adaptively change their representations based on task demands, enabling more flexible and generalizable problem-solving capabilities.

currentGrants.title: SEA-CROGS: Scalable, efficient and accelerated causal reasoning operators, graphs and spikes for earth and embedded systems
currentGrants.description: This project develops scalable causal reasoning methods for Earth system science and embedded applications. We create novel computational approaches that combine graph-based representations, spiking neural networks, and causal inference methods to analyze complex environmental data. The work aims to improve our ability to understand and predict Earth system dynamics while maintaining computational efficiency for deployment on resource-constrained platforms.

currentGrants.title: The next generation of operator regression networks: Theory, algorithms, applications
currentGrants.description: This project advances the theoretical foundations and practical applications of operator regression networks, a class of neural networks that learn mappings between function spaces. We develop new algorithms that improve the efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability of these networks. Applications include solving partial differential equations, modeling physical systems, and accelerating scientific computing across domains from fluid dynamics to materials science.

trainingGrants.title: Brown Postdoctoral Training Program in Computational Psychiatry
trainingGrants.description: This T32 training grant supports postdoctoral fellows at the intersection of computational neuroscience, machine learning, and psychiatry. The program trains the next generation of researchers to develop and apply computational methods for understanding psychiatric disorders, with emphasis on translating computational models into clinical insights. Fellows receive interdisciplinary training combining neuroscience, computer science, and clinical psychiatry.

completedGrants.title: Origins of Southeast Asian rainforests from paleobotany and machine learning
completedGrants.description: This collaborative project developed the Virtual Paleobotany Assistant (VPA), an AI tool using machine learning to rapidly analyze leaf fossil characteristics and assign specimens to plant families and orders. The VPA was used to interpret the origins of Southeast Asia's diverse tropical rainforests, which evolved during major continental movements. This unique collaboration between paleontologists and machine learning experts advanced both paleobotany methods and demonstrated AI applications in Earth sciences.

completedGrants.title: Intelligent spine interface (ISI)
completedGrants.description: This project developed an Intelligent Spine Interface to restore volitional control following spinal cord injury. The system interprets neural information from above a spinal lesion and transfers that information via artificial neural networks to sites below the lesion. Our contribution focused on developing state-of-the-art neural network architectures that could decode motor intent and generate appropriate stimulation patterns to restore lower limb function.

completedGrants.title: Leveraging computer vision to augment suicide risk assessment
completedGrants.description: This project applied computer vision and machine learning methods to clinical assessment of suicide risk. We developed algorithms to analyze behavioral cues and patterns that might indicate elevated risk, with the goal of augmenting traditional clinical assessment methods. The work explored how AI can support mental health professionals in identifying individuals who may benefit from intervention.

completedGrants.title: Oscillatory processes for visual reasoning in deep neural networks
completedGrants.description: This CRCNS US-France collaborative project investigated how synchronized neural oscillations in cortical networks support visual reasoning computations. We combined biophysical models, human electrophysiology, and deep learning to identify oscillatory components underlying human visual reasoning ability. The work developed novel machine learning idealizations of oscillatory neural processes that are trainable with modern methods yet interpretable at the neural circuit level.

completedGrants.title: Brain-inspired deep learning models of visual reasoning
completedGrants.description: This project identified perceptual principles and modeled brain mechanisms underlying human visual reasoning ability. We developed novel visual reasoning challenges to identify minimal necessary computations and systematically evaluated modern deep learning architectures. The work revealed that current networks struggle with abstract visual reasoning problems and developed brain-inspired mechanisms to address these limitations, advancing both neuroscience understanding and AI capabilities.

completedGrants.title: Next-generation machine vision for automated behavioral phenotyping of knock-in ALS-FTD mouse models
completedGrants.description: This project developed next-generation automated behavioral phenotyping methods for ALS-FTD mouse models using machine vision. We created sensitive, objective, and reproducible systems for continuous behavioral monitoring, enabling detection of earliest behavioral phenotypes. The work established procedures for remote video acquisition with cloud-based analysis, making these tools widely available to accelerate development of therapeutics for ALS-FTD.

completedGrants.title: Understanding the neural basis of the volitional state through continuous recordings in humans
completedGrants.description: This project analyzed continuous intracranial recordings from humans to understand neural mechanisms underlying volitional states. Using long-term recordings, we investigated how neural activity patterns relate to different states of volition and decision-making. The work provided insights into cortical dynamics supporting voluntary action and cognitive control in humans.

completedGrants.title: Automating pathology with deep learning
completedGrants.description: This project developed deep learning algorithms for analyzing histopathologic specimens to predict clinical outcomes in prostate cancer. We created algorithms to predict adverse pathologic features from biopsy specimens and biochemical recurrence from prostatectomy specimens. The work examined histopathologic features utilized by neural networks, identifying novel features that could improve traditional pathologic classification schemes and demonstrating both capabilities and limitations of AI in medical diagnosis.

completedGrants.title: Naturalistic data collection in the SmartPlayroom
completedGrants.description: This project designed a multi-sensor monitoring space called the SmartPlayroom for quantitative behavioral data collection in children. Equipped with mobile eye tracking, physiological sensors, and depth sensors, the space enabled automated analysis of movement kinematics, language, eye movements, and social interactions. The work demonstrated scientific advantages of naturalistic measurement and developed flexible computer vision algorithms for automated behavioral analysis in 4-9 year-old children.

completedGrants.title: WildCog: Evolution and local adaptation of cognitive abilities and brain structure in the wild
completedGrants.description: This interdisciplinary project investigated evolution of cognitive abilities in natural populations by combining measurements of fitness, cognitive performance, and neuroanatomy. We developed methods to link variation in cognitive functions to neurological structures in wild populations. The work provided unprecedented understanding of how selection operates on and shapes variation in cognition across species, advancing evolutionary neuroscience.

completedGrants.title: Scaling up computational models of visual processing in cortex
completedGrants.description: This DARPA Young Faculty Award and Director's Award project identified functionally relevant biophysically plausible computational mechanisms for visual cortex models. Rather than elaborate spiking neuron models, we developed novel mathematical idealizations that extend system-level models while remaining amenable to learning algorithms and interpretable in terms of biophysical mechanisms. This work bridged the gap between detailed biophysical models and state-of-the-art machine learning architectures.

completedGrants.title: Computational mechanisms of rapid visual categorization: Models and psychophysics
completedGrants.description: This NSF Early Career Award identified perceptual principles and modeled neural mechanisms underlying rapid visual categorization. By studying 'vision at a glance' before complex visual routines, the work developed a computational neuroscience model consistent with physiological properties of visual cortex cells that could predict human behavioral responses including correct and incorrect responses and reaction times across a range of conditions.

completedGrants.title: Development of a machine vision system for high-throughput computational behavioral analysis
completedGrants.description: This NSF I-Corps grant explored commercialization potential of machine vision systems for automated behavioral analysis. The project assessed market opportunities and customer needs for high-throughput behavioral phenotyping tools in pharmaceutical and academic research settings.

completedGrants.title: Towards a biologically-inspired vision system for the control of navigation in complex environments
completedGrants.description: This project developed neurally plausible models of visual perception for navigation with minimal sensing requirements. The work incorporated bottom-up and top-down cortical connectivity as well as mechanisms of 3D shape and motion processing to describe human performance in navigation tasks and underlying neural circuits, with applications to autonomous ground vehicle navigation.

completedGrants.title: Development of a machine-learning and computer-vision platform for automated behavioral analysis
completedGrants.description: This sponsored research project developed machine learning and computer vision platforms for automated analysis of animal behavior. The work created tools for high-throughput behavioral phenotyping that could be applied across various research and commercial applications.

completedGrants.title: Towards a human-level neuromorphic artificial visual system
completedGrants.description: This project created intelligent general-purpose cognitive vision algorithms inspired by the primate brain. The work explored how understanding and emulating information-processing strategies used in biological sensory systems could lead to substantial technological advances. Based on studying mechanisms of attention and object recognition in the primate brain, the project developed a new generation of neuroscience-inspired algorithms for computer vision.
